case.question: What can I serve that is easy for little hands to pick up?

retrieved.text: Offer varied family foods prepared for your child's abilities: soft cooked vegetables, ripe fruit, well-cooked eggs, mashed beans or lentils, and tender meat or fish with bones removed. Chop, mash or soften foods so they can manage them. Let them practise feeding themselves without pressure.
retrieved.title: What to feed your child

retrieved.text: 3 Sorting 2 objects • 4 cups and 4 spoons or 4 leaves and 4 sticks • Allow baby to play with objects • Show child how cups are the ‘same’ and spoons are ‘same’ • Mix up objects and ask child to put all the ‘same’ objects together • Praise child when finished! Play touch and bring game • Think of 3 objects in the house that child can easily get like shoe, cup, ball • Play a game and ask child to bring each object to you. • Praise child when he correctly gets object! • Ask child to say the name
retrieved.title: 3 Sorting 2 objects

retrieved.text: PLAY Give your child things to stack up, and to put into containers and take out. Sample toys: Nesting and stacking objects, container and clothes clips.
retrieved.title: 12 months up to 2 years: play
retrieved.source_title: Care for Child Development: Counselling Cards

records.answer:
Serve soft, bite-sized foods that are easy for little hands to grasp and self-feed. Here are four practical ideas:

1. Steamed carrot or sweet potato batons, cooked until tender enough to easily mash between your fingers.
2. Ripe banana slices or soft pear wedges.
3. Small, thin strips of plain omelette or soft scrambled eggs.
4. Well-cooked, short pasta shapes like fusilli or penne.

Always supervise mealtimes closely, and cut round foods like grapes or soft cooked vegetables lengthwise to reduce choking risks. Ensure pieces are small enough to manage safely.

Look for signs of hunger, (fuss, sucking/moving lips, opening mouth, making sounds, sticking out the tongue, putting hands in his mouth, making rapid eye movement before his/her eyes are open, baby may cry) • Breastfeed on demand (day and night, as often as the baby wants) at least 8 times in 24 hours. Frequent feeding produces more milk. • Breast milk is all your baby needs. • DO NOT give other foods or fluids

records.answer:
Before starting solids, early feeds should consist exclusively of breast milk or infant formula. These provide all the necessary nutrition and hydration required at this age. 

When feeding, always hold your baby close and in a comfortable, supported position. Never prop up a feeding bottle or leave your baby unattended with a bottle, as this creates a serious choking hazard. 

Solid foods and other liquids are not needed yet and should only be introduced around six months of age when your baby shows individual developmental readiness. If you have concerns about your baby's feeding patterns, weight gain, or nutrition, consult a qualified health professional or pediatrician for tailored guidance.

records.answer:
To help reduce milk dribbling back after a feed, try burping your baby gently during feeds and holding them upright while awake both during and after feeding. Ask a health professional about the best feeding positions for your baby. Always place your baby flat on their back to sleep; do not raise the head of the cot. 

Seek prompt medical assessment if the symptoms are painful or persistent, if there is poor weight gain, or if new symptoms appear. Seek urgent care immediately for forceful, green, or bloody vomit, if your baby is unable to keep fluids down, or if they refuse to feed.

records.answer:
Create a calming evening by keeping a familiar, quiet sequence as your baby grows. Dim the lights and use a soft voice during night care to signal the transition to sleep. 

Try these practical steps:
- Put on clean night clothes.
- Offer a gentle cuddle.
- Sing a soft lullaby.
- Speak in a quiet voice while holding or rocking your baby.

Reduce excitement and stimulation as bedtime approaches. Keep in mind that sleep patterns vary at this stage, so a calming routine helps set a peaceful atmosphere but does not guarantee uninterrupted sleep. Always place your baby on their back to sleep on a firm, flat surface with nothing else in the cot to keep them safe.

records.answer:
Create a calm, predictable wind-down sequence each evening by keeping activities quiet and familiar. Try these simple steps:

1. Change into fresh night clothes to signal that sleep is approaching.
2. Dim the lights in the room to help your child's body naturally wind down.
3. Share a quiet story together, sitting closely with a favorite book.
4. Keep interactions soothing and reduce exciting play as bedtime nears. 

Ensure that any items used during quiet time, such as small books or blankets, are kept free of small parts or hazards to maintain a safe environment. A consistent routine helps prepare your child for rest, though sleep patterns can still vary from night to night.

records.answer:
Yellowing of the whites of a newborn's eyes needs prompt professional assessment, as looking at colour cannot measure its severity. Contact a health worker or clinic promptly and tell them when the yellowing began, whether your baby's feeding has changed, and whether their urine is dark or stools unusually pale. Continue usual breast milk or infant formula feeds if your baby is able while arranging care. 

Seek emergency medical assessment right away if the yellowing appeared in the first day of life, or if your baby shows difficulty waking, is not feeding, has no wet nappies, experiences breathing problems, or shows abnormal stiffness. Do not attempt home treatment in sunlight. Keep your baby's head and neck fully supported whenever you hold them.

records.answer:
Keep your baby completely out of direct sun. Plan dense shade and dress them in loose, lightweight clothing that covers their arms and legs, along with a wide-brimmed hat to protect their head, ears, and neck. 

When on the move, attach a proper, breathable sunshade to the pram to block direct rays and maintain airflow; never drape a blanket over it, as this can quickly trap heat and cause dangerous overheating. Bring extra breast milk or infant formula to keep your baby well-hydrated in warm weather, offering feeds more frequently than usual. 

Avoid heavy layering, synthetic fabrics, and any sun-protection products unless specifically advised by a health professional. Check your baby regularly by feeling the back of their neck to ensure they are not getting too hot.

records.answer:
Soft fruits and well-cooked, mashed beans are suitable options alongside continued breastfeeding or infant formula, provided the baby can sit safely with a steady head and handle or swallow textures. 

Offer soft fruits—such as ripe banana or papaya—either peeled and mashed or cut into manageable, soft pieces. Beans should be thoroughly cooked and mashed or pureed to a smooth, soft consistency so they are easy to swallow. 

Always stay close and watch while the baby eats to keep mealtimes safe, encouraging them to sit still rather than moving around with food. Let the baby explore tastes at their own pace and stop when they show they have had enough.

case.question: Which vaccines are due for my child in Kenya?

records.answer:
Your child's recorded age is 9.0 months. Kenya's routine visits around your child's age:
- 9 months: Measles-rubella (MR) 1, IPV 2 and typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV); malaria vaccine 3 in eligible programme areas, and yellow fever vaccine in designated risk areas.
- 18 months: MR 2.

Malaria and yellow fever vaccines are not offered routinely in every area. Ask your vaccination clinic to confirm local eligibility and the malaria vaccine product in use.

Take your child's Mother and Child Health booklet or vaccination record to the clinic. These routine ages do not show which doses your child has already received or is due for; the clinic needs their record to confirm the next appointment.

records.answer:
You can practise taking turns by engaging in gentle, face-to-face moments while keeping your baby's head and neck fully supported.

- Gently stroke their skin or hands, then wait quietly to see how they respond before moving again.
- Sing a quiet line of a lullaby, then pause to listen to their breathing or soft sounds before continuing.

records.answer:
Celebrate turning one with these engaging, interactive activities:

• Talk and point: Ask your child simple questions, respond to their attempts to talk, and show and talk about nature, pictures, and things. Ensure any picture books used have sturdy cardboard pages to prevent tearing and choking hazards.
• Build together: Sit on the floor and stack soft blocks or plastic cups, then let your child knock them down. Use large blocks to prevent choking.
• Sing and move: Clap hands, sway to gentle music, and encourage simple dance movements. Keep the play area clear of sharp edges or tripping hazards.
• Explore textures: Let your child safely touch different everyday objects like a smooth wooden spoon or a soft piece of cloth while supervising closely to prevent mouthing small items.

records.answer: Begin tasting foods by offering small amounts of smooth, soft foods alongside breast milk or infant formula. Try options such as thick porridge, mashed vegetables, ripe fruit, or mashed legumes. Let your baby explore new tastes and flavours at their own pace. Watch closely for hunger and fullness signals, and never force food. If your baby rejects a new taste, stop and simply offer it again on another day. Always supervise your baby closely while eating to prevent choking, ensuring they are sitting upright with steady head and neck support.

records.answer:
Ongoing milk regurgitation after the first birthday needs an assessment by a health professional. Do not assume it is ordinary infant reflux, especially if there are concerns about feeding or weight gain. 

For basic care, keep your child upright for a short time after a feed and offer smaller, more frequent meals if recommended by a clinician, ensuring you do not change feed amounts or frequency without professional advice. 

Seek urgent medical care immediately if your child experiences forceful, green, or bloody vomit, is unable to keep any fluids down, shows signs of severe distress, or refuses to feed. A qualified healthcare provider should evaluate ongoing symptoms to determine the appropriate next steps.

records.answer:
Hold your baby gently and respond patiently, as crying is their way of communicating a need for closeness, comfort, or a check on ordinary needs. 

You can try these soothing steps:
* Speak in a soft, reassuring voice or hum a gentle tune.
* Use slow, steady rocking movements while holding them close.
* Engage through gentle touch and movement to help them feel secure.
* Check if they are too warm or uncomfortable in their clothing.

Ensure you always support your baby's head and neck securely when holding or moving them. Never shake or hit a child. If your baby seems unwell, experiences persistent crying, or cannot be consoled, seek advice from a qualified health worker.

case.question: My baby has loose watery stools. What should I watch?

retrieved.text: Hard, dry stools or painful straining can accompany constipation; the cause needs assessment, especially in a young baby. Discuss a new stool change with a health professional and describe feeding, wet nappies, stool appearance and discomfort. Keep formula at the packet's correct strength rather than changing the mix. Do not add water, solids, laxatives or remedies for a young infant based on chat. A very young baby who stops passing stool needs timely individual advice.

Inability to retain fluids, blood in stool, green or bloody vomit or a child becoming very unwell needs urgent assessment. Do not give diarrhoea-stopping medicine based on chat.
retrieved.title: Urgent advice

retrieved.text: Vomiting and diarrhoea can have several causes; chat cannot determine which applies. A baby can lose fluid quickly. Seek prompt medical advice if an infant has repeated vomiting or diarrhoea, particularly if feeding changes. Continue usual breast milk or correctly prepared formula if they can take it; do not dilute formula. Wash hands and clean soiled surfaces to reduce spread. Fewer wet nappies, stopping feeds or inability to keep fluids down need urgent care; green or bloody vomit also needs immediate assessment.

records.answer:
Continue offering your usual breast milk or infant formula regularly, and never dilute formula. Watch closely for signs that your baby is losing too much fluid. 

Seek prompt medical advice from a healthcare professional if you notice fewer wet nappies, if your baby stops feeding entirely, or if they are unable to keep fluids down. Also watch for lethargy, a sunken soft spot on the head, or any signs of fever. Wash your hands frequently and clean soiled surfaces carefully to help reduce the spread of germs.

records.answer:
Start with soft, simple textures such as thick porridge, mashed vegetables, ripe fruit, or well-cooked and mashed legumes, served alongside breast milk or infant formula. Let your baby explore new tastes at their own pace and stop when they show they have had enough. Keep mealtimes relaxed by offering small portions of varied, age-appropriate family foods and eating together when possible. 

Always stay with your baby while they are eating to prevent choking, and encourage them to sit still rather than running around with food. Avoid offering whole nuts, hard sweets, or foods that pose a choking hazard. If your baby persistently refuses food, shows difficulty or pain while eating, or refuses milk and fluids, consult a health professional promptly.

records.delivered_answer:
Serve finger foods cut into small, manageable pieces or soft sticks that fit easily in the palm. Great options include:

- Steamed carrot or sweet potato batons, cooked until tender enough to mash easily between your fingers.
- Ripe banana slices or soft, peeled pear wedges.
- Small cubes of very ripe avocado or well-cooked, low-sodium cheese.
- Well-cooked, small pasta shapes like penne or fusilli.

Always supervise mealtimes closely and ensure you remain seated nearby while eating to prevent choking. Cut round foods like grapes or cherry tomatoes lengthwise and into quarters, and avoid hard, raw vegetables, whole nuts, or sticky items that pose choking hazards.

Before around six months of age, early feeds should consist exclusively of breast milk or infant formula. These provide all the necessary nutrition your baby needs during this stage. Solid foods are not introduced until around six months, when your baby shows developmental readiness. 

If you are using infant formula, always prepare it strictly according to the manufacturer's instructions and hygiene guidelines to keep your baby safe. If you have any questions or concerns about your baby's feeding, consult a health professional for individual guidance.

records.delivered_answer: Begin with simple, soft foods like thick porridge, mashed vegetables, ripe fruit, or well-cooked legumes, continuing alongside breast milk or infant formula. Offer smooth textures initially and let your baby explore tastes at their own pace. Watch closely for hunger and fullness cues, and never force eating. To reduce choking risks, always stay close while your baby eats, ensure they are sitting upright with steady support, and offer small, appropriately textured bites. If a new food is rejected, simply try offering it again another day.

Serve finger foods cut into small, manageable pieces or soft sticks that fit easily in the palm. Great options include:

- Steamed carrot or sweet potato batons, cooked until tender enough to mash easily between your fingers.
- Ripe banana slices or soft, peeled pear wedges.
- Small cubes of very ripe avocado or well-cooked, low-sodium cheese.
- Well-cooked, small pasta shapes like penne or fusilli.

Always supervise mealtimes closely and ensure you remain seated nearby while eating to prevent choking. Cut round foods like grapes or cherry tomatoes lengthwise and into quarters, and avoid hard, raw vegetables, whole nuts, or sticky items that pose choking hazards.

retrieved.text: Looking after yourself It is important to take care of yourself. Being kind and patient with yourself will help you stay calm and be kind and patient with others. Here are some things you can try: • Keep in touch with family and friends, with a phone call if you can’t visit. • Try and rest when your child is resting, and try to get enough sleep at night. • If you feel stressed or angry take some long deep breaths. • Take short breaks. Get a glass of water or cup of tea and sit somewhere to drink it. Find things that help you relax and smile, maybe a funny TV show. • Limit how much you listen to the news if it is upsetting. • Tell family members or friends how you are feeling. Don’t be afraid to ask them for help so that you can have some time for yourself. • Before you go to sleep try and remember something your child did today that made you smile or feel good. Think of things that went well or people who were kind to you.

If using an age-suitable teething ring, follow its instructions; chill only as directed in a fridge, never a freezer, and never tie it around the child's neck. Supervise anything put in the mouth. Ask a health professional about persistent or worrying symptoms rather than choosing gels or medicines here.
delivered_references.title: Teething rings; comforting your baby

delivered_references.text: Drooling, chewing and a sore gum may accompany tooth eruption, but they do not prove that other symptoms are teething. There is no evidence that teething causes diarrhoea. Seek professional advice for fever, illness or symptoms that worry you instead of attributing them to teeth.
